subtype: Toddler cries, points and single words [Expressing]
passage: Under the neem tree, Jatin, two, began to cry, fists tight. His mother Amandeep checked in turn. "Hungry?" She held out a piece of roti; he pushed it away. "Thirsty?" He drank a little and kept crying. Then he rubbed his eyes and dropped his head on her shoulder. "Sleepy," she said, and rocked him. If the crying kept up or worried her, she would ask the doctor, but this time he slept.

qa.q: What did Jatin do when Amandeep offered the roti?
qa.a: He pushed it away.

qa.q: What does Jatin's rubbing his eyes and dropping his head suggest, and what else might the crying have meant?
qa.a: It suggests he was tired and needed sleep. The same crying could also have meant thirst or discomfort, which is why Amandeep checked each.

qa.q: What is a good way to respond to an unclear toddler cry?
qa.a: Check the likely needs one after the other, such as food, drink, sleep and comfort, and see a doctor if it keeps going or worries you.

qa.q: What might Jatin have felt when his first signals were not understood?
qa.a: He may have felt frustrated, since the roti and water did not fit what he needed.

grounding: A toddler cries, pushes away and rubs eyes, and the adult checks needs in turn.

subtype: Toddler cries, points and single words [Expressing]
passage: On the Sydney ferry Chidi, two, started whimpering and pointed at his father's bag. "More," he said. Jin handed him a cracker; Chidi threw it on the deck and wailed. Jin offered water, which Chidi pushed away. Then Chidi tugged at his ear and lay against Jin's arm, eyes half closed. "You're tired," said Jin softly, and held him. If it went on or worried him, he would check with a doctor.

qa.q: What did Chidi say when he pointed at his father's bag?
qa.a: He said "More."

qa.q: What might Chidi's tugging his ear and half-closed eyes suggest, and what else could it mean?
qa.a: They suggest he was tired and wanted to rest against his father. Tugging an ear can also signal discomfort, which is why Jin would check with a doctor if it kept up.

qa.q: What could Jin do to help Chidi settle?
qa.a: He can keep holding him quietly and give him time to sleep, having ruled out food and water for now. 🙂

qa.q: How might a passenger see the wailing?
qa.a: They may think it is simply a fussy child, but Jin's calm checking shows the cry had a real need behind it.

grounding: A toddler signals need with crying, pointing and pushing away, and the same cry can mean several needs that adults check in turn.

subtype: Toddler cries, points and single words [Expressing]
passage: I'm Raghav, from the flat next door. On Sunday I heard Rehana crying on the balcony for a long time. Her mother tried a biscuit; Rehana pushed it away. "No!" Then water. Another push. Then her mother checked her nappy. Still crying. Then she picked Rehana up and rocked her, and Rehana's head dropped onto her shoulder. She was asleep in two minutes. It was just tiredness. Her mother had tried everything in turn.

qa.q: What did Rehana's mother try first?
qa.a: A biscuit.

qa.q: What was Rehana likely feeling while she cried?
qa.a: She was very tired, which is why she refused the biscuit and water and fell asleep once rocked.

qa.q: What was wise about the mother's approach?
qa.a: She checked each need in turn, food, water, nappy and then comfort and sleep, instead of guessing once.

qa.q: How does Raghav experience the long crying?
qa.a: Raghav hears it with some concern and then feels relief, and seems to admire the mother's patience.

grounding: A neighbour sees a mother check food, drink, nappy and comfort in turn until she finds her toddler's crying is tiredness.

subtype: Toddler cries, points and single words [Expressing]
passage:
Monday: Rajni cried and pointed at the fridge. "More!" Irfan gave her yogurt, and the crying stopped.
Wednesday: she cried again and pushed the yogurt away. "No!" Irfan checked the time. Past her nap. He took her to bed, and she slept.
Saturday: she cried, holding her foot. "Ow!" Irfan found a thorn from the garden in her heel, took it out gently and cleaned it.

qa.q: What did Irfan find in Rajni's heel?
qa.a: A thorn from the garden.

qa.q: What was Rajni feeling behind each day's crying?
qa.a: On Monday she was hungry, on Wednesday tired, and on Saturday in pain from the thorn.

qa.q: What habit helped Irfan find the right need?
qa.a: He looked at her words and gestures, "more", "no" and "ow", and checked food, sleep and her body in turn.

qa.q: What would change if Irfan had offered yogurt every time?
qa.a: He would have missed that she was tired or hurt, and she would have stayed upset.

grounding: Over a week a father learns that his toddler's crying can mean hunger, tiredness or pain, and checks each in turn.

subtype: Toddler cries, points and single words [Expressing]
passage:
At Pune station, the train was late. Vijay started to cry on the bench, a whiny, on-and-off cry.
"Hungry?" Pallavi held out a banana. "No!" He pushed it away.
"Tired?" She patted her lap. He shook his head, still crying, and pointed at her bag.
She pulled out the water bottle. He grabbed it with both hands. "More!" He drank and drank, and the crying stopped.

qa.q: What did Vijay point at?
qa.a: Pallavi's bag.

qa.q: What was Vijay feeling, and how did Pallavi find out?
qa.a: He was thirsty and uncomfortable; she checked food and rest first, then followed his point to the water.

qa.q: What made Pallavi's approach effective?
qa.a: She checked possible needs one by one and watched his pointing and words.

qa.q: What would change if Pallavi had scolded Vijay for crying in public?
qa.a: His thirst would have gone unmet, and he would have cried harder.

grounding: A mother checks food, rest and drink in turn until her toddler's pointing and "more" show he is thirsty.

subtype: Toddler cries, points and single words [Expressing]
passage:
“Why is Kamal crying again?” asked Abbu.
“Let me check,” said Rehana. “Kamal, more?” She held up a biscuit. He pushed it away.
“Water?” He shook his head and cried harder.
“Sleepy?” He'd napped well. She felt his forehead. “Not hot.”
Kamal pointed down and wailed. “Owie!”
Rehana looked. His new sandal strap was pressing a red line into his foot.
“Oh, jaan! That hurts.” She unbuckled it, and the crying stopped.

qa.q: What was pressing a red line into Kamal's foot?
qa.a: His new sandal strap.

qa.q: What was Kamal feeling as he pointed down and wailed?
qa.a: He was in pain from the tight strap, and frustrated that his crying wasn't understood at first.

qa.q: What did Rehana do that helped her find the cause?
qa.a: She checked food, drink, sleep and temperature in turn, and then followed Kamal's pointing to his foot.

qa.q: How did Abbu see Kamal's crying at first?
qa.a: Abbu seemed puzzled and a bit weary, asking why Kamal was crying again.

grounding: It illustrates a toddler signalling a need through crying, pushing away, pointing and a single word, with an adult checking possible needs in turn.
